blocks.title: Chemical Coordination And Integration
blocks.text:
• Neural system provides a point to point, rapid coordination among organs.
  • As the nerve fibers do not innervate all cells of the body and cellular function need continuous regulation, hence the endocrine system integrates with the neural system for regulation and co-ordination.

blocks.title: Endocrine Glands and Hormones
blocks.text:
• Endocrine glands do not have ducts and are therefore known as ductless glands. They release chemicals known as hormones.
  • A hormone is a substance produced by endocrine glands, released into the bloodstream, and transported to a distant target organ.

blocks.title: Chemical Nature of Hormones
blocks.text: CHEMICAL NATURE OF HORMONES

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Hormone types and their roles can vary widely across species.

  • Hormones are regulated by feedback mechanisms (e.g., negative feedback for thyroid hormones or blood sugar control by insulin and glucagon).

blocks.title: Question 1
blocks.question:
A hormone is :-

(1) An enzyme

(2) Chemical messenger

(3) Primary messenger

(4) Both (2) and (3)
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(4) Both (2) and (3)

Explanation:

  • A hormone is a chemical messenger that is secreted by endocrine glands and transported via the bloodstream to target organs to regulate physiological processes.
  • Hormones are also considered primary messengers because they directly carry signals from glands to their target cells.
blocks.prompt: A hormone is :-

blocks.title: Question 2
blocks.question:
Statement not correct for hormones is that, these:-

(1) Are not all protein

(2) Are secreted in small amount

(3) Affect metabolism

(4) Acts as catalyst
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(4) Acts as catalyst

Explanation:

  • Hormones are not catalysts. Catalysts (like enzymes) speed up chemical reactions without being consumed, whereas hormones regulate physiological processes by binding to specific receptors on target cells. They do not directly catalyze reactions.
blocks.prompt: Statement not correct for hormones is that, these:-

blocks.title: Question 3
blocks.question:
First discovered hormone :-

(1) Thyroxine

(2) Adrenaline

(3) Secretin

(4) Insulin
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(3) Secretin

Explanation:

  • Secretin was the first hormone to be discovered in 1902 .
  • It is a hormone released by the small intestine (duodenum) that stimulates the pancreas to release bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize stomach acid.
blocks.prompt: First discovered hormone :-

blocks.title: Hypothalamus
blocks.text:
• The hypothalamus, located at the base of the diencephalon in the forebrain, plays a crucial role in regulating various body functions.
  • It contains numerous neurosecretory cells known as nuclei that produce neurohormones.
  • These neurohormones control the production and release of hormones from the pituitary gland.

blocks.title: Pituitary Gland
blocks.text:
●       Pituitary located in a bony cavity called Sella Tursica

●       Attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.

blocks.title: The Pineal Gland
blocks.text:
• Located on the dorsal side of the forebrain.

• Secretes – Melatonin hormone.

• Plays a very important role in the regulation of 24 hours (diurnal rhythm).

• Maintaining the normal rhythm of the sleep-wake cycle.

• Regulation of body temperature.

• Influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and as well as defense capability.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• The pineal gland is known for secreting melatonin to regulate sleep-wake cycles, it also influences seasonal rhythms in some organisms.
  • Mixing up the functions of the hypothalamus, pituitary, and pineal glands, since all are part of the endocrine system.
  • Ignoring the clinical importance of these glands in conditions like hypothyroidism (due to pituitary issues), sleep disorders (pineal gland), and hormone imbalances (hypothalamic dysfunction).

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The posterior pituitary gland is not a 'true' endocrine gland because :-

(1) It is under the regulation of hypothalamus

(2) It secretes enzymes

(3) It is provided with a duct

(4) It only stores and releases hormones
blocks.answer:
Answer- 4

The correct answer is:

(4) It only stores and releases hormones

Explanation:

  • The posterior pituitary gland is not considered a "true" endocrine gland because it does not produce hormones. Instead, it stores and releases hormones (such as oxytocin and vasopressin/antidiuretic hormone, ADH) that are produced by the hypothalamus.
  • These hormones are synthesized in the hypothalamus and transported to the posterior pituitary via nerve fibers, where they are stored until needed.
options: (1) It is under the regulation of hypothalamus
(3) It is provided with a duct
(4) It only stores and releases hormones
blocks.prompt: The posterior pituitary gland is not a 'true' endocrine gland because :-

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Which one of the following hormones, though synthesised elsewhere, is stored and released by the master gland ?

(1) Melanocyte stimulating hormone

(2) Antidiuretic hormone

(3) Luteinizing hormone

(4) Prolactin
blocks.answer:
Answer- 2

The correct answer is:

(2) Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)

Explanation:

  • Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is synthesized in the hypothalamus but stored and released by the posterior pituitary gland (part of the "master gland").
  • The hypothalamus produces ADH and oxytocin, which are then transported to the posterior pituitary for storage and later release into the bloodstream.
blocks.prompt: Which one of the following hormones, though synthesised elsewhere, is stored and released by the master gland ?

blocks.title: Question.3
blocks.question:
Acromegaly is caused by :-

(1) Excess of S.T.H.

(2) Excess of Thyroxine

(3) Deficiency of Thyroxine

(4) Excess of Adrenaline
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is: 1
Explanation:

  • Acromegaly is a hormonal disorder caused by the excess secretion of growth hormone (GH), also called Somatotropic Hormone (STH), from the pituitary gland  in adulthood.
  • It results in abnormal growth of bones in the hands, feet, and face.
  • When STH is overproduced before puberty, it leads to gigantism, characterized by excessive height due to long bone growth.
blocks.prompt: Acromegaly is caused by :-

blocks.title: Question.4
blocks.question:
Hypophysis cerebri is the other name of :-

(1) Adenohypophysis

(2) Islets of langerhans

(3) Neurohypophysis

(4) Pituitary
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is: 4

Explanation:

  • The hypophysis cerebri is another name for the pituitary gland, a small endocrine gland located at the base of the brain, beneath the hypothalamus.
  • The pituitary gland is often called the "master gland" because it controls the secretion of hormones from other endocrine glands.
blocks.prompt: Hypophysis cerebri is the other name of :-

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.text:
• The thyroid gland comprises two lobes on either side of the trachea.
  • Both lobes are interconnected with a thin flap of connective tissue called isthmus (non-glandular part).
  • Origin: Endodermal
  • Position: Located in the neck between the trachea and larynx.
  • Structure: 'H' shape, Largest Endocrine gland.

blocks.title: Function of Thyroid Hormone
blocks.text:
• Regulation of BMR
  • Erythropoiesis
  • Regulates metabolism of carbohydrates,protein and fats.
  • Maintenance of water and electrolytes.
  • Play an important role in the development of CNS.
  • Promotes DNA replication cell division → growth
  • Menstrual cycle

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing thyroid hormones: Mistaking T3 (triiodothyronine) for T4 (thyroxine). T3 is the more active form, while T4 is a precursor converted into T3 in the body.
  • Assuming hypothyroidism is only due to underactive thyroid: Secondary hypothyroidism can be caused by pituitary or hypothalamic issues, not just by thyroid dysfunction.
  • Not considering the role of calcitonin: Many focus on thyroid hormones (T3, T4) but overlook calcitonin, which helps regulate calcium levels in the blood.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
Artificial light, extended work-time and reduced sleep–time disrupt the activity of

(1) Thymus gland

(2) Pineal gland

(3) Adrenal gland

(4) Posterior pituitary gland
blocks.answer:
Answer- 2

The correct answer is:

(2) Pineal gland

Explanation:

  • The pineal gland secretes melatonin, a hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle (circadian rhythm).
  • Artificial light, extended work hours, and reduced sleep interfere with melatonin production, disrupting the circadian rhythm and affecting sleep patterns.

blocks.title: Question- 2
blocks.question:
Which of the following conditions results from hypothyroidism in adults?

(1) Gigantism
(2) Myxedema
(3) Acromegaly
(4) Tetany
blocks.answer:
Answer: (2) Myxedema
Explanation:
Hypothyroidism in adults leads to myxedema, characterized by lethargy, weight gain, dry skin, and puffiness, due to reduced levels of thyroid hormones.

blocks.question:
The thyroid gland is located:

(1) In the brain
(2) In the thoracic cavity
(3) On either side of the trachea
(4) Near the pancreas
blocks.answer:
Answer: (3) On either side of the trachea
Explanation:
The thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped gland located in the neck, on either side of the trachea, just below the larynx.
options: (3) On either side of the trachea

blocks.title: Parathyroid Gland
blocks.text:
• Origin: Endodermal
  • Position: Present on the backside of the thyroid gland. Four in number (One pair for each lobe of the thyroid gland).
  • The parathyroid gland secretes parathyroid hormone (PTH), Collip's hormone, or parathormone.
  • It is a polypeptide in nature.

blocks.title: Functions of Parathyroid Glands
blocks.text:
• An increase in blood calcium level causes Hypercalcemia
    • A decrease in blood phosphate level causes Hypophosphatemia
    • Parathormone is essential for survival as it is critical in maintaining homeostasis by regulating calcium and phosphate ion levels in the extracellular fluid (ECF).

blocks.title: Thymus Gland
blocks.text:
• Origin :- Endodermal
  • Position:- The thymus gland is a lobular structure (bilobed) located between the lungs behind the sternum on the ventral side of the aorta.
  • Hormone secrete:- Thymosin.
  • Nature of thymosin:- Proteinaceous.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• PTH increases blood calcium levels, while calcitonin (secreted by the thyroid gland) decreases blood calcium levels.
    • The thyroid regulates metabolism and growth, while the thymus is involved in the development of the immune system, specifically T-cells.
    • The thymus is essential for the differentiation and maturation of T-lymphocytes (T-cells), which are key components of the adaptive immune system.

blocks.title: Question- 1
blocks.question:
What happens in the body when there is hypersecretion of PTH?

1. Hypocalcemia

2. Hypercalcemia

3. Increased calcitonin levels

4. Increased blood phosphate levels
blocks.answer:
Answer: (2) Hypercalcemia
Explanation: Hypersecretion of PTH leads to excessive calcium release from bones and increased calcium absorption, resulting in hypercalcemia (high blood calcium levels).

blocks.title: Question- 2
blocks.question:
The thymus gland is largest and most active during which stage of life?

1. Infancy and childhood

2. Adolescence

3. Adulthood

4. Old age
blocks.answer:
Answer: 1. Infancy and childhood
Explanation: The thymus gland is largest and most active during infancy and childhood, as it is crucial for the development of the immune system. Its activity declines after puberty, and it gradually shrinks in size.

blocks.title: Question- 3
blocks.question:
What is the primary function of parathyroid hormone (PTH)?

1. Decrease blood calcium levels

2. Increase blood calcium levels

3. Stimulate thyroid hormone secretion

4. Regulate sodium and potassium balance
blocks.answer:
Answer: (2) Increase blood calcium levels
Explanation: PTH increases blood calcium levels by stimulating calcium release from bones, enhancing absorption in the intestines, and reducing calcium excretion by the kidneys.

blocks.answer:

Explanation: The thymus gland is responsible for T-cell development and differentiation. B-cells are developed and matured in the bone marrow, not the thymus.

blocks.title: Adrenal Gland
blocks.text:
• They are also called suprarenal glands or glands of emergency.
  • Our body contains a pair of adrenal glands, one positioned on top of each kidney. Each gland is made up of two distinct types of tissues—
(i) The centrally located tissue is called the adrenal medulla

(ii) Outside this lies the adrenal cortex

blocks.title: Control of Adrenal Secretion
blocks.text:
• ACTH of the anterior pituitary controls the secretion of the adrenal cortex (mainly glucocorticoids).
  • Secretion of mineralocorticoids is controlled by Renin (Kidney).
  • The nervous system controls adrenal medullary hormones.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
Which of the following hormones is secreted by the adrenal medulla?

(1) Cortisol
(2) Epinephrine
(3) Aldosterone
(4) Thyroxine
blocks.answer:
Answer: (2) Epinephrine

Explanation:

  • Epinephrine (also known as adrenaline) is secreted by the adrenal medulla. It plays a key role in the body’s response to stress by increasing heart rate, blood flow to muscles, and breaking down glycogen to glucose for quick energy.
  • Cortisol and Aldosterone are secreted by the adrenal cortex.
  • Thyroxine is produced by the thyroid gland.
blocks.prompt: Which of the following hormones is secreted by the adrenal medulla?

blocks.title: Question- 2
blocks.question:
Which of the following is NOT a function of cortisol?

(1) Increases blood sugar levels
(2) Suppresses immune system activity
(3) Helps in stress response
(4) Regulates sodium balance
blocks.answer:
Answer: (4) Regulates sodium balance

Explanation:

  • Cortisol, a glucocorticoid hormone from the adrenal cortex, increases blood sugar levels, suppresses immune responses, and helps the body cope with stress.
  • Aldosterone is responsible for regulating sodium and water balance in the body, not cortisol.
blocks.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a function of cortisol?

blocks.title: Question- 3
blocks.question:
Which of the following is NOT a part of the adrenal glands?

(1) Adrenal cortex
(2) Adrenal medulla
(3) Adrenal capsule
(4) Adrenal duct
blocks.answer:
Answer: (4) Adrenal duct

Explanation:

  • The adrenal glands are composed of the adrenal cortex (outer layer) and the adrenal medulla (inner part).
  • There is no adrenal duct; the adrenal glands are ductless endocrine glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
  • The adrenal capsule is the outer covering of the adrenal glands.
blocks.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a part of the adrenal glands?

blocks.title: Question-4
blocks.question:
Which hormone is primarily responsible for the regulation of sodium and water balance in the body?

(1) Cortisol
(2) Adrenaline
(3) Aldosterone
(4) Insulin
blocks.answer:
Answer: (3) Aldosterone

Explanation:

  • Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex. It helps regulate sodium and potassium levels in the blood and maintains blood pressure by controlling water retention.
  • Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone that affects metabolism and helps in stress response.
  • Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal medulla and is involved in the fight-or-flight response.
  • Insulin is produced by the pancreas and regulates blood glucose levels.
blocks.prompt: Which hormone is primarily responsible for the regulation of sodium and water balance in the body?

blocks.title: Pancreas
blocks.text:
• Origin: Endodermal
  • Position: Elongated organ situated between the limbs of the 'C' shaped duodenum.
  • Nature: Heterocrine / Mixed / Composite gland / Compound (exocrine and endocrine).
  • The exocrine portion secretes an alkaline pancreatic juice containing enzymes, and the endocrine portion secretes hormones, insulin and glucagon.

blocks.title: Disorder of Pancreas
blocks.text:
Diabetes mellitus

  • Prolonged hyperglycemia (High level of blood glucose)
Reason: Hyposecretion of insulin (deficiency of insulin) and insulin resistance

  • Loss of glucose through urine (glycosuria)
  • Formation of ketone bodies (keto acidosis) and presence of ketone bodies in urine (ketonuria)
  • Diabetic patients successfully treated with insulin therapy.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
Which of the following hormones secreted by pancreas ?

(1) Insulin and glucagon

(2) Epinephrine and nor-epinephrine

(3) Thyroxin and melanin

(4) Prolactin and oxytocin
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(1) Insulin and glucagon

Explanation:

  • Insulin and glucagon are the primary hormones secreted by the pancreas. These hormones are produced by the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
  • • Insulin helps lower blood glucose levels by promoting the uptake of glucose into cells.
      • Glucagon raises blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to release stored glucose (glycogen).
blocks.prompt: Which of the following hormones secreted by pancreas ?

blocks.title: Question- 2
blocks.question:
The islets of Langerhans are found in :

(1) Pancreas

(2) Stomach

(3) Liver

(4) Alimentary canal
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(1) Pancreas

Explanation:

  • The Islets of Langerhans are clusters of cells found in the pancreas. These cells are responsible for producing important hormones like insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin, which regulate blood sugar levels and other metabolic processes.
  • • Insulin and glucagon are particularly important for regulating blood glucose.
blocks.prompt: The islets of Langerhans are found in :

blocks.title: Gonads
blocks.text:
• A pair of testis is present in male individuals' scrotal sac (outside abdomen).
  • The testis serves dual roles as both a primary sex organ and an endocrine gland. It is composed of seminiferous tubules and interstitial (or stromal) tissue.
Hormone- Testosterone:

  • Regulates development, maturation and function of the male accessory sex organ
  • Stimulates muscular growth
  • Growth of facial and axillary hair
  • Increases aggressiveness
  • Low pitch of voice
  • Stimulates spermatogenesis
  • Acts on CNS and influence the male sexual behavior (libido)
  • Produce anabolic effect on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

blocks.title: Hormone-Estrogen
blocks.text:
• Produce mainly by growing ovarian follicles
  • Stimulates growth and activities of female sex organs
  • Development of growing follicles
  • Appearance of female secondary sex characters (high pitch voice)
  • Development of mammary glands
  • Regulate female sexual behaviour

blocks.title: Hormone- Progesterone
blocks.text:
• Support pregnancy
  • Acts on the mammary glands and stimulates formation of alveoli and milk secretion

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Testosterone is produced by the Leydig cells in the testes throughout life, but its levels significantly increase at puberty.
    • Estrogen is primarily produced by the ovaries, but small amounts are also produced by the adrenal glands and placenta during pregnancy.
    • LH triggers ovulation in females and stimulates the Leydig cells to produce testosterone in males.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
Leydig cells are meant for :-

(1) Formation of sperm

(2) To produce progesterone

(3) To produce testosterone

(4) Nutrition of sperm
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(3) To produce testosterone

Explanation:

  • Leydig cells are located in the testes and are responsible for producing testosterone, the primary male sex hormone. Testosterone is essential for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics and plays a crucial role in spermatogenesis (sperm production).

blocks.title: Mechanism of Hormone Action
blocks.text:
• There are two types of hormones: (i) water-soluble hormones and (ii) lipid-soluble hormones.
  • Hormones exert their effects on target tissues by binding to specific proteins known as hormone receptors, which are found only in those tissues.
  • Receptors located on the cell membrane of target cells are called membrane-bound receptors, while those located inside the target cell are known as intracellular receptors, often found in the nucleus.
  • When a hormone attaches to its receptor, it creates a hormone-receptor complex. Each receptor is specific to a single hormone, ensuring precise interactions.
  • The formation of this complex triggers biochemical changes in the target tissue, thereby regulating its metabolism and overall physiological function.

    • The thymus is essential for the differentiation and maturation of T-lymphocytes (T-cells), which are key components of the adaptive immune system.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Testosterone is produced by the Leydig cells in the testes throughout life, but its levels significantly increase at puberty.
    • Estrogen is primarily produced by the ovaries, but small amounts are also produced by the adrenal glands and placenta during pregnancy.
    • LH triggers ovulation in females and stimulates the Leydig cells to produce testosterone in males.

blocks.title: The Pineal Gland
blocks.text:
• Located on the dorsal side of the forebrain.

• Secretes – Melatonin hormone.

• Plays a very important role in the regulation of 24 hours (diurnal rhythm).

• Maintaining the normal rhythm of the sleep-wake cycle.

• Regulation of body temperature.

• Influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and as well as defense capability.
